chunk_findings.detail: The config change puts a template placeholder into the gate command itself (`command = "uv run pytest tests/ -q --timeout=420 -n {workers}"`), but only `data["command"]` is ever substituted. `operations.py` builds the payload from `show_full, full = full, gate.command if gate else ""` and passes `full` (i.e. the raw `gate.command`, now containing `{workers}`) into `_selection_data(...)`; that helper receives no config object, so it cannot substitute anything, and therefore `data["full_suite"]` is still the literal string `uv run pytest tests/ -q --timeout=420 -n {workers}`. The line below only blanks it when `show_full` is false, so when the whole‑suite command is requested (`ddflow tests --full`, i.e. `show_full=True`, which the adjacent comment says is "the merge queue's and the phase end's" command) the emitted/consumed command carries `{workers}` verbatim. Demonstration: run `ddflow tests <item> --full`; `data["full_suite"]` ends in `-n {workers}`, and any consumer that executes it (or even just uses it as the parity/evidence command) hands pytest `-n {workers}`, which pytest-xdist rejects as an invalid int, so the whole-suite run cannot start. The same `full` value is also reused for the "full" command shown in the gate evidence, so the placeholder can leak there too. The substitution needs to be applied to every command string built from `gate.command` (at minimum `data["full_suite"]`/`full`), not only `data["command"]`.

chunk_findings.detail: `_TEST_FILE.search()` matches on any token, so option *values* that merely name a test file are counted as if they were selected tests. `shlex.split("... --ignore=tests/test_slow.py tests/")` yields the single token `--ignore=tests/test_slow.py`, whose suffix `/test_slow.py` matches `(?:^|/)(?:test_[^/]*|[^/]*_test)\.py$`, so `count_test_files` returns 1 even though the command selects a whole directory. `compute` then executes `n = min(n, files)` (line 72), so a command like `pytest -n {workers} --ignore=tests/test_slow.py tests/` gets `-n 1` on a quiet 192-core host that would otherwise compute dozens of workers. The same false positive hits `--deselect tests/test_a.py::test_x` (the `(?:::.*)?` suffix even makes node ids match) and any other flag whose value ends in `_test.py`/`test_*.py`; exclusions are not workload, and the cap should be derived from selected files only (or from counting .py tokens that are not attached to an option).

chunk_findings.detail: The load-unavailable fallback `n = min(hi, UNKNOWN_LOAD_WORKERS)` never applies the lower bound, so it can return fewer than `[ci].min_workers` and break the documented clamp. With `ci.min_workers = 24`, `ci.max_workers = 48`, and a `SignalSource` whose `sample()` has no `"load"` key, `load is None` takes this branch and returns `n = 16`, below the configured minimum (the memory branch is not reached either unless `free` is present). The fallback should be `max(lo, min(hi, UNKNOWN_LOAD_WORKERS))` to preserve the `[min, max]` invariant.

chunk_findings.detail: Every other test in this file pins the machine input through the `run()` helper (`cores=192`), but this one calls `WK.resolve(cmd, cfg(), source=src)` with no `cores` argument, and `cfg()` carries no `cores` field. `resolve` must therefore read the core count from the host itself, so the substituted count is a function of the machine running the suite. With `source = FakeSource({"load": 0.0, ...})`, `load_per_core.high = 0.75`, and `min_workers = 1`, a 2-core runner computes `floor(2 * 0.75 - 0.0) = 1`, so `resolve` returns `"pytest -n 1 tests/test_a.py tests/test_b.py"` (1 < the 2 selected files, so the file cap does not raise it back to 2), and the assertion `cmd == "pytest -n 2 tests/test_a.py tests/test_b.py"` fails. Since the feature is explicitly meant to adapt to small/busy machines, the worker count produced by `resolve` needs to be pinned by injecting cores (or by having `resolve` accept a cores argument), otherwise this test is non-hermetic and goes red on 1–2 vCPU runners/containers.

chunk_findings.detail: The new clamp is only applied where the file count is threaded through, and it is missing for the unit_tests gate command. `WK.resolve` takes the bound as its third argument — the line above passes `len(files)`, but the gate line calls `WK.resolve(data["unit_tests_gate"]["command"], cfg)[0]` with no file count, so the upper bound "never above the number of selected test files" ([D-agent-test-etiquette], and the `[ci].workers` doc in the same diff) does not hold for that command. Given an idle 192-core host and an item whose `unit_tests_scope` selects 2 test files, `ddflow tests <item>` resolves the main `data["command"]` with `len(files)=2` (2 workers) while the gate command is resolved load-only and gets `max_workers=48`, so `-n {workers}` becomes `-n 48` for a 2-file scope; running that same command (the substituted gate command is also what the gate executes) starts 48 xdist workers for 2 files. If the intent is that only per-invocation commands are file-bounded, the gate path still reads the *selected* item's files, which is exactly the count the clamp is supposed to use.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/operations.py (the `data["unit_tests_gate"]["command"] = WK.resolve(...)` line)

chunk_findings.detail: The builder no longer returns a runnable command. Before this change the emitted worker argument was the self-contained token `-n auto`, so the string returned by `pytest_command_for_files(root, py_tests)` could be executed (or `shlex.split` and run) by any caller. Now it returns a template containing the bare token `{workers}` that only works if the caller performs the workers substitution first. The failure input is any project that declares pytest-xdist with a serial unit_tests/ci command and whose returned command is executed without going through `services/workers.py` (e.g. the affected-tests runner built from the same selected-file list, a dry-run/evidence print, or any other existing caller of this function): pytest receives `-n {workers}` and aborts with `argument -n: invalid value: '{workers}'`, which previously worked as `-n auto`. Because the returned value is documented as the command ("its runner prefix … and its options … are kept, the path arguments are replaced by the selected files"), either the substitution has to happen inside this function (which already has `py_tests` in hand) or every consumer must be shown to substitute; embedding a template literal in a value that is otherwise an executable command is a regression for the unsubstituted paths.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/testselect.py (`return shlex.join([*cmd, *py_tests]).replace("'{workers}'", "{workers}")`)

chunk_findings.detail: The fixed-override branch returns `N` immediately, skipping the "never above the number of selected test files" cap (and the load/memory logic). `files` is even placed into the `inputs` dict on line 45, so the branch returns a record that visibly contradicts itself. Demonstration: with `[ci].workers = 16` and a gate command that selects a single file (e.g. `pytest tests/test_a.py`), `resolve` computes `files = 1` and then `compute` returns `n = 16`; the auto path (`files=1`) would have been capped to `n = 1` by `n = min(n, files)`. The intent states the count must be "at least 1, never above the number of selected test files", and the module docstring repeats "never above the number of test files", so 16 workers for a one-file selection violates the specified invariant.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/workers.py:46-48 (`compute`, the `if setting != "auto"` early return)

chunk_findings.detail: The `or "auto"` fallback is unreachable for the most common "unset" value because `str()` is applied first: `str(None).strip().lower()` is `"none"`, which is neither `"auto"` nor `.isdigit()`, so the next branch sets `n = 1`. Demonstration: an empty YAML value (`[ci].workers:` → `None`) or a null from the config loader yields `"none"` → `if setting != "auto"` is taken → `n = int("none")` is skipped by the `isdigit()` guard → `Workers(1, ...)`, silently pinning the gate to a single worker instead of computing from the machine, i.e. the opposite of the "must not be a fixed -n / calculate at run time" requirement. Only the empty string `""` triggers the intended `"auto"` default; `None`/`False`/`0`-as-null all fall through to fixed `1`.

chunk_findings.detail: Every timing assertion in this file is an *upper* bound, so the tests cannot distinguish "waited, then gave up at the bound" from "gave up instantly the moment a holder was seen". Take an implementation whose poll loop returns the `blocked`/exit-2 result as soon as `_holders()` is non-empty (i.e. `_bounded` computes a limit that `wait` never actually honours, or the conflict branch short-circuits before sleeping): test 1 still sees elapsed ≈ 0.01 s < 10, `exit == 2`, `woke == False`, `holders[0]` = T1/agent-holder, and the reason strings all pass; test 2 (`timeout_s=0.2`) passes with no elapsed check at all; test 3 likewise. So the whole premise of the change — a *bounded wait* that waits up to `max_s`/`timeout_s` before declaring itself blocked — is unverified: no test asserts that a run with a live holder took at least ~`min(timeout_s, max_s)`, nor that a wait whose holder releases before the bound wakes with exit 0. Given `timeout_s=600, max_s=0.3` in test 1 and `timeout_s=0.2` in test 2, the fix is a lower-bound assertion (e.g. `assert 0.3 <= elapsed < 10`) plus a release-and-wake case.

At `t = 20` the lock is acquired, `pre.mark == log.mark(clock=False)` still holds, so `act` becomes `pre.activity(act)` and `act(L)` returns `-400` → L is judged idle and broken while its holder was active 5s ago. Before this change the probe ran under the lock and saw `t = 15`, so no break. The window is exactly the lock wait, so it widens with contention, and the outcome is destructive (a live lease is broken and its worktree can be taken over).

chunk_findings.detail: The mark guard re-verifies only the event log, never the activity watermark that actually decides idleness. `_prejudge` fills `pre.seen` from `LB.tree_activity` before the lock is taken, and `_break_idle` then judges from those stored values (`act = pre.activity(act)`); `pre.mark == log.mark(clock=False)` only tells you the *log* did not move, and the docstring says exactly that (`mark` is "the log's fingerprint"), so a worktree write by the other agent is invisible to the re-check. Concrete run: `[lease].hold_max_s = 900`; agent B holds lease L in worktree W with last activity 1000 s ago when `_prejudge` probes it, so `seen[L] = T0-1000`. The pre-pass then runs the activity git probes for the remaining clashing leases and/or waits for the append lock, which can take seconds; during that window B writes into W and is live again. B's write appends no log event, so under the lock `pre.mark == log.mark(clock=False)` still holds and `_break_idle` computes `now - seen[L] = 1000 >= 900`, judges L idle and breaks it. Before this change the probe ran under the lock (`act = activity or LB.tree_activity(log.root)` immediately before the verdict), so the fresh mtime would have been seen and L would have been refused. The failure direction is one-sided and destructive: a stale (smaller) watermark can only make an active lease look idle, i.e. `claim --break` can now clobber a lease whose holder just resumed work. Either re-probe activity under the lock for the leases actually put in the break plan, or treat a watermark as valid only if nothing could have touched the worktree since it was taken.

chunk_findings.detail: The earlier finding (reusing pre-read worktree watermarks as though the event-log mark proved them current) is only partly answered: `fresh` now bounds how *old by the wall clock* the reading may be, but it still does not detect that the worktree changed between the pre-read and the lock. Concrete interleaving: `hold_max_s = 300`, lease `L` held by `A`, last worktree activity at `t = -400s` (idle), log quiet. At `t = 0` `_prejudge` stores `pre.seen[L] = -400` with `pre.at = 0`; the append lock is held by another writer; `A` resumes at `t = 0.5s` (new commit/edit — `LB.tree_activity` is `git log`/`status`, so this appends nothing to the log, or at most a renewal). At `t = 1s` `_break_idle` takes the lock, `pre.fresh(1.0)` → `1.0 - 0.0 <= 5.0` → True, so `act = pre.activity(act)` and `L` is judged from the `-400` reading and broken — a lease with fresh progress is broken. The window is not closed, only capped at `FRESH_S`; any lock wait shorter than 5s (the normal case, and exactly the contention case this change targets) judges on a snapshot that the holder can have invalidated. The author's probe does not answer this: `test_a_stale_worktree_reading_is_probed_again_rather_than_trusted` sets `FRESH_S = -1.0`, which forces the predicate to `False` and merely tests the re-probe plumbing; it never exercises a reading that is clock-fresh but worktree-stale, which is the residual wrong-break case. A fix that actually answers the finding needs a signal that the worktree moved (e.g. re-probe when the log moved or when the pre-read is older than the wait it is meant to cover), or the git read must stay under the lock.
